<sub>See also [`http-server/a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs`](http-server.md#http-server-a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs), [`http-server/a-trailing-slash-is-never-normalised`](http-server.md#http-server-a-trailing-slash-is-never-normalised), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs"></a>

## A CORS preflight is answered from `[http.cors]` before the unit is loaded, and a plain `OPTIONS` is passed through

`rule:http-server/a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs`

A CORS preflight — an `OPTIONS` carrying both `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` — is answered from `[http.cors]` **before any application code runs and therefore before the compiled unit is loaded**. The response policy owns that decision and it is closed by default, so with nothing configured a preflight is a `403`: the verb is one the server implements, and what is refused is the origin, not the method.

That is the one point in a request's life at which the server genuinely has no route table to ask. Everything afterwards runs with the unit in hand, and the unit carries the table, which is what lets the server match once ([`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler)) and what the CSRF check reads ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default)). Answering the preflight here is also what keeps it honest: an application asked to answer an `OPTIONS` would be answering a question the policy above it had already decided, and the two could disagree.

A plain `OPTIONS` — missing either header — is not a preflight and is **passed through** rather than answered. An application that wants to answer one has `Core\Router::methodsFor` for the `Allow:` header, and which convention to adopt stays its choice rather than the server's.

<sub>See also [`http-server/head-runs-as-get`](http-server.md#http-server-head-runs-as-get), [`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`http-server/cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named`](http-server.md#http-server-cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named).</sub>

<a id="http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps"></a>

## `[limits] request_body` bounds bytes parsed into memory and `upload_total` bounds a streamed multipart body, each with a hard ceiling, and a route that never reads a body allocates nothing

`rule:http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`

Two caps bound a request body, each a `Runtime` default with a `[limits.hard]` ceiling — the existing pair gaining two rows, not a third instance of the pattern ([`config/ceilings-are-their-own-directives`](config.md#config-ceilings-are-their-own-directives)). `[limits] request_body` bounds **bytes parsed into memory**, at `"8M"` with a `"64M"` ceiling; `[limits] upload_total` bounds a **streamed multipart body**, at `"256M"` with a `"2G"` ceiling. Because `Core\Request::body()` is a call, the body is read on demand: a route that never reads one allocates nothing, and a route may raise its own cap before reading. A body over `request_body` is refused; the same body on a route that raised its cap first is accepted. The reader throws `RuntimeError` and the request records it, so under `Core\Router::dispatch` a handler that throws after it is answered `413` through the gate's `refused` with `BodyTooLarge` ([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)). It costs one `bool` per request.

**An uploaded file is a stream, and `Core\Request::files(): Iterable<Part>` is the only way to receive one.** There is no temp file — no `tmp_name`, no `move_uploaded_file`, no temp directory to configure, permission or clean up after a crash — because where a part lands is an application's explicit call under `fs.write` ([`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream)), never the runtime's default.

`Core\Request::bodyStream(): Iterable<bytes>` is the raw-body reader, for a body larger than a request's memory budget or a content type `files()` does not describe. It yields `tainted` chunks and is a **streaming** reader, so it keeps nothing, consumes the body, and may only be the first reader of it — [`http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it`](http-server.md#http-server-buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it) is which readers may follow which, for every member that reads a body. It is bounded by `request_body` on what a consumer retains, by the connection's `body_idle_timeout`, and by the multipart part-count cap ([`errors/multipart-part-count`](errors.md#errors-multipart-part-count)), which no byte cap bounds.

<sub>See also [`http-server/four-idle-waits-all-finite`](http-server.md#http-server-four-idle-waits-all-finite), [`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream), [`errors/multipart-part-count`](errors.md#errors-multipart-part-count), [`config/ceilings-are-their-own-directives`](config.md#config-ceilings-are-their-own-directives), [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources), [`http-server/a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename), [`http-server/there-is-no-temp-file`](http-server.md#http-server-there-is-no-temp-file).</sub>

<a id="http-server-buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it"></a>

## A buffering body reader keeps what it read so another may follow it, and a streaming one consumes the body and is the only reader of it

`rule:http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it`

A request body is read either by a **buffering** reader — `Core\Request::body()`, `::bytes()`, `::post()`, `::json()`, `::jsonAs<T>()` — which keeps what it read, so another buffering reader may follow it; or by a **streaming** reader — `::bodyStream()`, `::files()` — which hands the octets to the program as they arrive, keeps none of them, and so consumes the body. A buffering reader fills the request's hold, bounded by `[limits] request_body` ([`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps)), and answers out of it: any buffering reader may follow any other, in any order, and each answers the same octets. A streaming reader may only be the first reader, and once it has run nothing reads those octets again.

| Reader | Kind | Keeps |
|---|---|---|
| `body()` | buffering | the octets |
| `bytes()` | buffering | the octets |
| `post()` | buffering | the octets and the fields it decoded — over a multipart body, the fields alone |
| `json()` | buffering | the octets, and the `Value` it decoded |
| `jsonAs<T>()` | buffering | the octets |
| `bodyStream()` | streaming | nothing |
| `files()` | streaming | nothing of a file part; the non-file fields, which it buffers |

A reader that arrives after the body was consumed throws `LogicError` naming the member that consumed it. It is refused rather than answered empty, because an empty answer from an exhausted stream is indistinguishable from a body that was empty, and that is the ambiguity [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused) exists to refuse. The refusal is a defect in the program, never something a peer can provoke.

**`post()` after `files()` is this rule rather than an exception to it.** A `files()` walk streams the file parts and buffers everything else: a multipart form's non-file fields are held as the walk passes them ([`http-server/a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename)), charged against `request_body` like any other buffered body, and `post()` answers out of that hold. It drains whatever the walk did not reach before answering, so it reports every field rather than the ones that arrived ahead of the part the walk stopped on — which is why a handler that wants the uploads takes `files()` first. `body()` after a walk is still refused: the hold carries the decoded fields, never the raw octets.

**A multipart body's hold is whichever reader filled it, and only one of the two kinds can hold the octets.** `post()` and `files()` parse such a body off the wire as it arrives, so what they leave behind is the buffered fields and `body()` after either is refused for the reason above. `body()`, `json()` and `jsonAs<T>()` hold the octets instead, under `request_body`, and a `post()` following one parses *those* rather than the wire, which is drained by then and would answer a form with no fields in it. Any buffering reader still follows any other; what the order changes is only which hold the request has. This is the two caps of [`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps) doing what they say rather than a case being carved out: a multipart body larger than `request_body` is read by `post()` and `files()`, which never hold one whole, and refused to `body()`, which does.

`json()` keeps its decoded `Value` because `Core\Json::decode` produces only arrays and scalars, and an array is copy-on-write, so a second caller can be handed a refcount bump safely. `jsonAs<T>()` keeps nothing beyond the octets and decodes per call, because `decodeAs` builds objects and two callers must never be handed the same one. `post()` keeps its parsed fields for the same reason as `json()`: a form parses to arrays and strings alone, so each later call is a lookup in it. **What this spends**, per [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority): the held octets, at most `[limits] request_body` per in-flight request — already `post()`'s bill before this rule — plus one decoded value for a request that called `json()` and one parsed form for a request that called `post()`. Both are freed with the request, so the cost is O(in-flight) and never O(requests served).

The kinds are not a roster to maintain: a member is buffering exactly when it fills the hold, which is a fact the runtime already has, so a body reader added later classifies itself. The alternative — a closed exclusive set of three members with `post()` and then `json()` each carved out of it — was rejected on the second carve-out, because two exceptions to a rule are the rule, unwritten.

**Declined:**
- **Adding `json()` and `jsonAs<T>()` to the exclusive set.** `json()` after `body()` would throw where nothing was consumed, and a handler that logs `body()` and then decodes `json()` is not a defect.
- **Re-reading the wire for a second buffering reader.** A body already off the wire cannot be read again, and answering empty instead is the ambiguity [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused) refuses.
- **Letting `bodyStream()` follow `body()` by replaying the hold.** The member would mean two things depending on what ran before it: bounded by the connection's idle timeout in one case and by nothing in the other. A streaming reader reads the wire or it is refused.
- **Deciding a reader's kind by `Content-Type`.** A mislabelled but valid document is read, as `post()` reads one, and the kind of a reader is a property of the member, never of the request.

<sub>See also [`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps), [`http-server/a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename), [`http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`](http-server.md#http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused), [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority).</sub>

<a id="http-server-static-serving-is-one-policy"></a>

## Static serving is one policy in both modes: the exact file, never a listing, one `ETag`, one `Range` checked by `If-Range`, a body streamed from disk, and a `.nvs` file is never served as source

`rule:http-server/static-serving-is-one-policy`

Static serving is one policy in both modes, because a second policy is a second security model. The exact file only, and **never a directory listing**; `index.html` is the sole default document; the MIME type comes from a fixed extension table and an unknown extension is `application/octet-stream`, which the response policy's `nosniff` renders inert. A file a program names with `Core\Response::sendFile` is answered by the same policy as a file a static mount selects.

**A static file answers `GET` and `HEAD` alone.** Any other method at a path step 3 selected is a bodiless `405` with `Allow: GET, HEAD`, before the file is opened, so a `POST` to a stylesheet is never answered as if it had written something. A verb outside the eight a program can name is still the door's `501`. `sendFile` is not judged by method: the program answering the request chose it.

Freshness is `Cache-Control: no-cache` with a strong `ETag` over `(size, mtime_nanos)` and `If-None-Match` — one validator, exact, and specifically **not** `Last-Modified`, whose one-second granularity serves stale bytes for two edits inside the same second. The tag and the bytes come from one opened file, so a file replaced between a stat and a read cannot pair one file's tag with another file's bytes.

A single `Range` is honoured; a multi-range request, a second `Range` line, a bound that is not ASCII digits alone (`+1`, a space), a unit other than `bytes`, or a range the file cannot satisfy is a `416` carrying `Content-Range: bytes */len`, never a silent `200` with the whole body. **`If-Range` is compared strongly against the current `ETag`**, read only when `Range` is present and after `If-None-Match`. A match honours the range; anything else — an old tag, a `W/` tag, an HTTP date, a value that does not parse — ignores the range and answers the whole file with a `200`, including a range that would otherwise be a `416`. A date never matches because this server sends no `Last-Modified`. That is what makes a resumed download safe: a client resuming a file that changed underneath it gets the new file whole, never the tail of one file spliced onto the head of another.

**A file body is streamed from disk, one chunk at a time.** `Content-Length` is exact and stated, so nothing is chunk-encoded, and a file that ends early or fails to read ends the body in an error that cuts the connection: a short body under a stated length would read as a whole file. A `HEAD` reads nothing. There is no configurable `max-age`, no `immutable` and no precompressed-variant lookup: this is a development convenience and a fallback, not a CDN.

**A stream that states its length gets the same decision.** `Core\Response::stream` with a `length` reads `If-None-Match`, `If-Range` and `Range` exactly as a file does, against the `etag` the program gives, and answers `304`, `206` or `416` by the same rules; the decision is one function both callers share. The program writes the window the decision gives (`Core\Response\Stream::offset` and `length`), the count is exact, and a stream that ends before its window is full cuts the connection as a short file does. Without an `etag` neither validator matches; without a `length` the stream is chunked and `Range` is ignored.

**A `.nvs` file is never served as source**, under any dispatch, from any mount. **Nor is a file the program could not read by default:** a dot-file, a file in a dot-folder (`.well-known` included; a route answers it), `nvs.toml`, a `.nvst` test file, and a database file a `[db]` block names with its `-wal`, `-shm` and `-journal` files. Only the host tree has `[db]` blocks, since an `[[app]]` block has no `[db]` table, and a reload that moves one builds the table again. One predicate, `nvs_config::capability::kept_from_requests`, decides the first three for both. A declined file falls through to the next step, so the peer cannot tell it from a missing one. A link is followed to where it leads, and the file there is judged.

**An HTML, SVG or XML file is sent with `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; frame-ancestors 'none'`.** It runs no script and has no origin of its own, so a file somebody uploaded under a static root cannot act as the site. The cost is that a static page's own script does not run either: a page that needs script is rendered by a program. A program's own `setHeader` still has the last word on `sendFile`.

**In development, a request from a loopback address must name this machine in `Host`:** `localhost`, a name under `.localhost`, a loopback address, or a host a `[[server.mount]]` lists. Any other host reaches no mount and gets the table's `404`, and only the health probe answers it. That closes DNS rebinding, where a web page makes its own name resolve to `127.0.0.1`. A request from another machine is not asked, so a development server on `0.0.0.0` still answers its network address.

- **Memory:** one open file handle and one 64 KiB chunk per in-flight file response, plus the HTTP layer's write buffer, whatever the file's size or the range's. The next chunk is read only when that buffer has room, so a slow peer holds the read back. Nothing is cached between requests: O(in-flight), not O(files served).

**Declined:**

- **Refusing a hard link out of the root.** A containment check on the canonical path cannot see one, and refusing every file with more than one link would refuse files a package manager deduplicated. Making one needs write access to the root, which is already the whole deployment.
- **Reading the whole file or the whole range into memory.** A download of several gigabytes would hold several gigabytes per connection, and the first byte would wait for the last read.
- **A `Last-Modified` validator, or a date in `If-Range`.** One-second granularity serves stale bytes and splices a download edited twice in one second.
- **Serving the range when `If-Range` does not match.** The client would write the tail of a changed file onto the head of the old one.
- **A stream that writes from byte 0 and a server that drops the bytes before the range.** A seek near the end of a large stream would make the program produce everything before it.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-request-resolves-in-five-steps`](http-server.md#http-server-a-request-resolves-in-five-steps), [`http-server/an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect`](http-server.md#http-server-an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect).</sub>

<a id="http-server-health-path-is-off-and-checks-nothing"></a>

## `health_path` is off by default; set, it answers `200` while accepting and `503` while draining, and checks no dependency

`rule:http-server/health-path-is-off-and-checks-nothing`

`[server] health_path` is off by default, so no URL is silently reserved. When set it is matched ahead of every mount, answers `200` while the process is accepting and `503` while it is draining, with an empty body, and is skipped by the access log.

It performs **no dependency checks** — a health endpoint that pings the database converts a slow database into a simultaneous outage across every instance — and reports no version or build information. A built-in probe reports that the *process* is alive even when the application fails to compile, where an application-route probe would fail and produce a restart loop that cannot fix a compile error. A start where some mounts do not compile is alive by this probe too, while those mounts answer `500` ([`http-server/a-mount-table-expands-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-a-mount-table-expands-at-boot)); `nvs service status` names them.

`Core\Server::isDraining()` gives an application the same bit for an endpoint of its own; a program that is not being served reads `false`, which is the answer rather than an error. What draining does to the connections still open is [`concurrency/a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly).

<sub>See also [`http-server/the-server-block-is-boot-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-server-block-is-boot-class), [`concurrency/a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly).</sub>

<a id="http-server-the-access-log-is-a-mode-default"></a>

## `[log] access` is a mode default — on in development, off in production — and a `5xx` other than `501` is logged whatever it says

`rule:http-server/the-access-log-is-a-mode-default`

`[log] access` is one of the five `Runtime` defaults a mode selects ([`config/a-mode-is-five-defaults`](config.md#config-a-mode-is-five-defaults)): `true` in development, `false` in production. In production an access line is a third copy of a fact the proxy's log and the root span already hold, written with request-path I/O; in development there is no proxy and traces are sampled, so it is the most useful thing the server prints.

It renders through the one diagnostic record — text in development, JSON in production ([`errors/renderings`](errors.md#errors-renderings)) — and there is deliberately **no Common or Combined Log Format**, which would be a second renderer. The fields are `method`, `path` (never the query string), `status`, `durationMs`, `bytes` where the body's length is known when the head goes out, `clientIp`, `route` when the application matched one, and the trace id as the envelope's `request_id` ([`errors/log-fields`](errors.md#errors-log-fields)). An access line is `Info`. The health probe writes no line, whatever its status.

**An error is logged unconditionally**, whatever `access` says: a `5xx` is a diagnostic rather than access telemetry, and losing one because access logging was off would be the wrong failure. It is written at `Error`, so the production default level keeps it. A `501` is the exception and is an access line like a `4xx`: the door answers it to a verb the client made up, so an error line per `501` would let any client write one per request.

The door writes the line where it counts the request for the request series, so every answer it writes has one — a refusal at the valve and a mount table's `404` included. `access` is read off the snapshot the request ran under, so an `[[app]]` block's own value and a reload reach the next request; a program's `Core\Config::set` of it changes nothing, because the line is written after the request's own view has gone. An answer the door wrote before a request carrier existed has no trace id on its line.

<sub>See also [`observability/a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request`](observability.md#observability-a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request), [`http-server/health-path-is-off-and-checks-nothing`](http-server.md#http-server-health-path-is-off-and-checks-nothing), [`config/a-mode-is-five-defaults`](config.md#config-a-mode-is-five-defaults), [`errors/log-fields`](errors.md#errors-log-fields), [`errors/renderings`](errors.md#errors-renderings), [`observability/the-runtime-exports-what-it-already-measures`](observability.md#observability-the-runtime-exports-what-it-already-measures).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address"></a>

## `[log] client_ip = false` keeps the client address out of every record the server writes, and `Core\Request::clientIp()` still returns it

`rule:http-server/a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address`

`[log] client_ip` is `true` by default, and `false` keeps the client address out of every record the
server writes: the access line, the `5xx` line that is written whatever `access` says, and every
diagnostic about a forwarded header. The field `clientIp` is left out of those lines, not written as
`null`, so a reader cannot mistake a removed address for a request that had none. Spans and metrics
carry no client address in either setting. `Core\Request::clientIp()` returns the address as before,
because a program that limits a rate or checks an allow-list needs it in memory, and what it writes
to its own log is its own code.

It is a `System` directive, applied at reload. A request that could turn it back on would undo the
promise an operator made to the people whose addresses these are, so only the file sets it.

Why it exists: an operator who promises that no address is stored needs a setting that holds for every
line, including the `5xx` line [`http-server/the-access-log-is-a-mode-default`](http-server.md#http-server-the-access-log-is-a-mode-default) writes
unconditionally. Turning the access log off is not enough. The telemetry collector is the first program
that makes this promise ([`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address)).

- **Memory:** none. The setting removes one field from a record that is written anyway.

**Declined:**
- **A masked address, such as the first three bytes of an IPv4 address.** It is a second format to
  get right for IPv6 and for every proxy shape, and a masked address is still personal data in many
  places. An operator who wants the address keeps it whole, and one who does not leaves it out.
- **Leaving the address out of `Core\Request::clientIp()` too.** The program then cannot limit a rate
  per address at all, and the setting is about what is written, not what is known for one request.

<sub>See also [`http-server/the-access-log-is-a-mode-default`](http-server.md#http-server-the-access-log-is-a-mode-default), [`http-server/trusted-proxies-is-empty-and-empty-reads-nothing`](http-server.md#http-server-trusted-proxies-is-empty-and-empty-reads-nothing), [`errors/log-fields`](errors.md#errors-log-fields), [`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address).</sub>

<a id="http-server-secure-headers-with-nothing-written"></a>

## A deployment that wrote no `[http.headers]` already sends `nosniff`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` and a referrer policy on every response

`rule:http-server/secure-headers-with-nothing-written`

Every response the server writes carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a
`Content-Security-Policy` of `frame-ancestors 'none'`, and `Referrer-Policy:
strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, with no `[http.headers]` block present. The block's fields are
the shipped values, and a written block is read field by field: `false` or the empty string drops
a header, and a value the wire cannot carry falls back to the shipped default rather than to
nothing.

There is no default `Content-Security-Policy` beyond `frame-ancestors`. A `default-src` policy
that is wrong breaks the page silently and is the most abandoned security header there is, while
a policy that is right is application-specific; `frame-ancestors 'none'` is the one directive
safe for every application, because it governs who may frame the response rather than what the
response may load. The XSS half of what a CSP buys is closed structurally by
[`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape), which does not depend on being configured.

A header the response already wrote is left alone
([`http-server/policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins`](http-server.md#http-server-policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins)), and HSTS is the one
member of the set with a condition of its own ([`http-server/hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme`](http-server.md#http-server-hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme)).

**Declined:**
- **A full default `Content-Security-Policy`.** A wrong CSP breaks the page with no diagnostic,
  which is how CSP gets disabled for good after one incident. Framing is the safe subset, and it is
  the one shipped; a further default waits for a shape that is safe for every application.
- **A nonce or hash the server adds to every `<script>`, `<style>` and inline handler the developer
  wrote.** Escaped holes already keep injected markup out of a page
  ([`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape)), so it would add protection only to a hole in a URL, an
  `on*` handler or a script body. Finding those needs the HTML position model
  [`core-classes/html-template`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-template) declines, and a fragment fetched by script carries its own
  response's nonce, which never matches the page's.

<sub>See also [`http-server/hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme`](http-server.md#http-server-hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme), [`http-server/policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins`](http-server.md#http-server-policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins), [`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape).</sub>

<a id="http-server-hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme"></a>

## HSTS is emitted when the effective scheme is `https` and not otherwise, and `hsts_subdomains` defaults to `false`

`rule:http-server/hsts-follows-the-effective-scheme`

`Strict-Transport-Security` is emitted when the effective scheme is `https`, and not otherwise. A
browser ignores it on a plaintext connection, so emitting it there is noise; and because the
server never terminates TLS itself, the effective scheme is the one a *trusted* proxy asserts
through `X-Forwarded-Proto`. With `trusted_proxies` empty the scheme is `http` and no HSTS is
sent — the safe direction for a header that cannot be revoked from a client. `localhost`,
`127.0.0.1` and `::1` are secure contexts in every current browser, so local development over
plain HTTP is unaffected.

The max-age is `[http.headers] hsts`, shipped as `365d`, and `false` disables it.
`hsts_subdomains` defaults to `false`.

**Declined:**
- **`hsts_subdomains = true` by default.** `includeSubDomains` is the HSTS setting that has
  actually taken deployments down: a sibling subdomain on plain HTTP becomes unreachable for the
  max-age, with no way to revoke it from the client, and whether every subdomain is TLS-only is
  knowledge the runtime does not have.

<sub>See also [`http-server/secure-headers-with-nothing-written`](http-server.md#http-server-secure-headers-with-nothing-written), [`http-server/trusted-proxies-is-empty-and-empty-reads-nothing`](http-server.md#http-server-trusted-proxies-is-empty-and-empty-reads-nothing), [`http-server/two-deployments-and-nothing-a-proxy-owns`](http-server.md#http-server-two-deployments-and-nothing-a-proxy-owns).</sub>

<a id="http-server-cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named"></a>

## CORS is closed until `[http.cors] origins` names one: no header is emitted and a preflight is answered `403`

`rule:http-server/cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named`

With `[http.cors] origins = []`, which is the shipped value, no CORS header is emitted at all and
a preflight is answered `403`. That is what closed means, and it is the correct default because
a browser's same-origin policy is doing its job until somebody deliberately relaxes it.

Naming an origin opens exactly that origin: a matching `Origin` is echoed back and the answer
varies on it, a non-matching one gets nothing, and a preflight from a named origin is granted with
what the block configures — `methods` (shipped `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`), `headers`, `expose`,
`credentials` and `max_age`. An origin is matched exactly and never normalised. `["*"]` answers
everybody without varying, and is permitted only beside `credentials = false`
([`http-server/a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused)).

A plain `OPTIONS` and a cross-origin `GET` are not preflights and are handed to the route. A
route that needs its own policy sets it for itself, request-locally
([`http-server/policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins`](http-server.md#http-server-policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins)).

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused), [`http-server/policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins`](http-server.md#http-server-policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused"></a>

## `origins = ["*"]` with `credentials = true` is refused at boot and at runtime alike, and so is `same_site = "None"` without `secure`

`rule:http-server/a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused`

`origins = ["*"]` together with `credentials = true` is refused — at boot as `E0612` naming the
line, in [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one)'s diagnostic shape,
and at runtime by `Core\Config::set` returning `false` and leaving the value unchanged
([`config/a-refused-set-returns-false`](config.md#config-a-refused-set-returns-false)). Refused rather than warned, because the combination
is not risky: it is meaningless. Every browser rejects it, so a deployment that wrote it has an
access-control policy that does not do what it says and no signal that it does not.

`[http.cookies] same_site = "None"` with `secure = false` is refused by the same mechanism for the
same reason — browsers reject the pair, so it is a policy with no meaning rather than a weak one.

The two mechanisms are held to one implementation of each condition: the guard asserts that boot
and `Core\Config::set` *agree* over a table of moves into and out of each pair, rather than
asserting what either answered on its own.

**Declined:**
- **A warning instead of the refusal.** The configuration has no correct meaning to warn about, and
  a boot warning is read once.

<sub>See also [`http-server/cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named`](http-server.md#http-server-cors-is-closed-until-origins-are-named), [`http-server/cookies-are-secure-httponly-and-lax`](http-server.md#http-server-cookies-are-secure-httponly-and-lax), [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`config/a-refused-set-returns-false`](config.md#config-a-refused-set-returns-false).</sub>

<a id="http-server-cookies-are-secure-httponly-and-lax"></a>

## Every cookie `Core\Response::addCookie` writes is `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` unless the call site says otherwise

`rule:http-server/cookies-are-secure-httponly-and-lax`

`[http.cookies]` ships as `secure = true`, `http_only = true`, `same_site = "Lax"`, `path = "/"`,
and every `Core\Response::addCookie` call inherits each field it did not write. So a cookie
written with no options bag is `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`, and a cookie that
genuinely needs to be readable by script says so at the call site, in one field, visibly —
omitting `HttpOnly` and nothing else.

The options bag carries the same four settings as booleans and a `SameSite` enum in
[`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type)'s shape, never the string the directive uses
([`core-api/shape-rules`](core-api.md#core-api-shape-rules) R11). A fourth `same_site` spelling in the file is refused rather
than read as one of the three, and `"None"` without `secure` is refused outright
([`http-server/a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused)).

A cookie's *name* is not this rule's business: [`errors/cookie-name-bytes`](errors.md#errors-cookie-name-bytes) owns it — a name
matches byte for byte with no substitution, and `__Host-` and `__Secure-` semantics are enforced
on read and on write. The two rules meet at the same header and are otherwise independent.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wildcard-origin-with-credentials-is-refused), [`errors/cookie-name-bytes`](errors.md#errors-cookie-name-bytes), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type), [`core-api/shape-rules`](core-api.md#core-api-shape-rules).</sub>

<a id="http-server-policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins"></a>

## Every `[http.headers]`, `[http.cors]` and `[http.cookies]` directive is `Runtime` class, and `Core\Response::setHeader` overrides a policy-owned header on one response without logging

`rule:http-server/policy-headers-are-runtime-class-and-setheader-wins`

Every directive under `[http.headers]`, `[http.cors]` and `[http.cookies]` is
[`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes)' **`Runtime`** class: `nvs.toml` states the default a
request starts with, a request may set any value for itself through `Core\Config::set`, and the
change is discarded when the request ends ([`config/a-runtime-set-is-request-local`](config.md#config-a-runtime-set-is-request-local)). The next
request on the same core sees the configured value. `Core\Response::setHeader` additionally
overrides a policy-owned header on **one** response with no configuration involved at all: a
header the response already carries is left alone when the policy set is filled in.

This costs nothing in security because the alternative buys nothing. A request can already write
any response header it likes through `setHeader` — that is what a response object is. A
compromised handler can therefore turn its own response's protections off, and could before any
of these blocks existed. Per-request override is what keeps the policy usable: an API route with
its own CORS policy and an embeddable route that permits framing are both ordinary, and neither
needs a second configuration mechanism.

A policy-owned header replaced through `setHeader` is **not** logged.

**The framing headers are not policy, and `setHeader` throws `LogicError` for them.** `Content-Type`
is the body member's ([`security/response-body-is-one-typed-member`](security.md#security-response-body-is-one-typed-member)). `Content-Length`,
`Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection` and `Upgrade` are the server's: it writes each from the body it
sends and the connection it holds. `hyper` frames a body by a `Content-Length` it is handed, so a
program's that disagrees with the body desynchronises the connection, a response split with no
newline in it. The server drops a declared framing header too, so a declaration that reaches it
some other way changes nothing.

**Declined:**
- **`RuntimeTighten` policy blocks.** Narrowing-only would forbid the legitimate case (one API
  route with an open CORS policy beside an application that has none) while stopping nothing.
  `RuntimeTighten` is for grants, where "may drop rights, never add them" is the whole mechanism
  ([`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes)); a response header is not a grant.
- **Logging an override.** The header is ordinary output the request wrote deliberately, and a
  line per response on any route that customises one is noise that trains people to ignore the log.
- **Admitting a `Content-Length` that matches the body.** The server already writes that value,
  so the only `Content-Length` a program could add is a wrong one.

<sub>See also [`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes), [`config/a-runtime-set-is-request-local`](config.md#config-a-runtime-set-is-request-local), [`http-server/secure-headers-with-nothing-written`](http-server.md#http-server-secure-headers-with-nothing-written).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations"></a>

## A session is a record its store issued: a backend answers `issue`, `load`, `save` and `destroy`, and `load` answering absent is the whole of the strict-id rule

`rule:http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`

A session is one record in a store that can answer *did I issue this id*. A backend answers four
operations and no more: `issue` mints an identifier this store has never issued, writes an empty
record under it and answers the id; `load` answers the record under an id, or **absent**; `save`
replaces the record under an id, refreshing its expiry; `destroy` forgets it.

**`load` answering absent is the whole of the strict-id rule.** An id the store did not issue, one
it issued and has since expired, and one an attacker minted are the same answer, and `start`
responds to all three identically: discard it and `issue` a fresh one. There is no separate
`validateId`, because a second question is a second thing that can disagree with the first. A
presented id that is not 22 base64url characters is absent by construction, before any round trip.

The identifier is 128 bits from the CSPRNG `Core\Crypto` draws from, rendered base64url — not a
counter and not a hash of anything the client supplied: an id is a bearer credential for the
length of its life, and the only property it needs is that guessing one is not a strategy. The
record crosses the store boundary as the byte carrier a `Core\Cache` entry does
([`concurrency/a-cached-value-is-copied-across-the-boundary`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-cached-value-is-copied-across-the-boundary)). `start` is the one member that
talks to the store ([`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster)).

**Declined:**
- **A signed cookie holding the record itself, with no store.** It costs no round trip, but a store
  that holds nothing cannot answer *did I issue this id*
  ([`security/a-session-id-the-store-did-not-issue-is-rejected`](security.md#security-a-session-id-the-store-did-not-issue-is-rejected)). A logged-out session would
  stay valid until its own expiry, and the record's size limit would be a cookie header's.
  `Core\SignedCookie` remains for an application that wants exactly this.

<sub>See also [`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster), [`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly), [`http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot), [`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store), [`concurrency/a-cached-value-is-copied-across-the-boundary`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-cached-value-is-copied-across-the-boundary).</sub>

<a id="http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot"></a>

## `[session] backend` admits `shared` and `db`, and writing `memory` is a boot refusal naming the file it was written in

`rule:http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`

```toml
[session]
backend = "shared"      # or "db", the default; there is no third value
ttl     = "2h"          # how long an untouched record survives; the store enforces it
cookie  = "nvsid"       # the name the identifier rides under
```

`shared` is the coherent tier reached at `[cache.shared] url`
([`config/cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store`](config.md#config-cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store)); `db` is the SQLite file
`session.sqlite` in the data folder, and the store a tree that writes no `backend` gets
([`http-server/no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store`](http-server.md#http-server-no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store)). `backend = "memory"` is `E0626`,
and its note says what that store loses — a request another server process handles finds no
session, and a restart deletes every one — and names the file the key was written in. That is what
"enforced rather than documented" means: the value is refused where it is written, not where it is
used, so a deployment cannot be running on a session store held in one process while believing
otherwise. A generic unknown-value refusal would not do it: an operator who wrote `memory` because
`Core\Cache::memory()` is the fast store needs the sentence explaining why the fast answer is the
wrong one. Any other word gets the same code with a note naming the two that are admitted. The
note's text is `REFUSED_NOTE` in `crates/nvs-config/src/session.rs`.

The roster is a type with no memory variant, and every store operation is written against the shared
tier's connection or the SQLite file rather than the tier enum, so the process's map is absent rather
than merely unselected. The key is `System` class ([`config/system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it`](config.md#config-system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it)),
because where a fleet's sessions live is a deployment decision. It reloads: a request reads the block
from the snapshot it cloned, so a changed backend reaches the next request, and no record moves from
the old store to the new one, which signs every user out.

`shared` costs a session one round trip on a read and two on a write, and `db` one statement on the
blocking pool for each. That is latency spent to buy security and request isolation: the memory tier
would cost none, and it is refused because a session there is not coherent across processes and does
not survive a restart ([`concurrency/the-memory-tier-cannot-hold-what-must-be-coherent`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-memory-tier-cannot-hold-what-must-be-coherent)). `db` is
coherent across the processes of one machine, and `shared` across machines.

**Declined:**
- **A directory of files, one per session.** A file cannot expire itself and a directory has no index
  on expiry, so the sweep is a walk over every file. The SQLite file has both, and its sweep is one
  indexed delete ([`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store)).

<sub>See also [`concurrency/the-memory-tier-cannot-hold-what-must-be-coherent`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-memory-tier-cannot-hold-what-must-be-coherent), [`http-server/no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store`](http-server.md#http-server-no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store), [`config/cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store`](config.md#config-cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store), [`config/system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it`](config.md#config-system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it), [`core-api/two-cache-tiers`](core-api.md#core-api-two-cache-tiers).</sub>

<a id="http-server-no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store"></a>

## A tree with no `[session] backend` keeps its sessions in a SQLite file in the data folder, and `start` throws naming `[session]` where there is no data folder

`rule:http-server/no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store`

A tree that writes no `[session] backend` gets the `db` store: `session.sqlite` in Novis's own data
folder ([`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults)), in WAL mode. A first
program that calls `Core\Session::start` needs no configuration. Every server process on the machine
that shares the data folder reads the same file, so a request another process handles finds the
session, and a restart keeps it. That is the reason the memory tier is refused
([`http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot)), and the file
meets it. `shared` stays the store for several machines.

A process with no usable data folder, one that could not be created or failed
[`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)'s check, has no default store. There `start` throws a
`RuntimeError` naming `[session] backend = "shared"`, and every other member throws until `start`
has run ([`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly)).

The file is Novis's own: the operator chose the folder, the name is fixed, and no program-supplied
path reaches it. So no capability is asked, as none is for the compiled-code cache beside it. Each
operation is one short statement in its own transaction, so two requests of one session never wait
for each other ([`http-server/a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole)). `busy_timeout`
covers the moment two writers meet, and that wait is one statement long.

- **Memory:** one SQLite connection and its statement cache per core, O(cores), and nothing per
  session served. The rows are on disk, O(live sessions), because expired rows are swept
  ([`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store)).
- **Latency:** one indexed read at `start` and one upsert for a changed record, each on the blocking
  pool, so a core never waits on the disk ([`http-server/a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall`](http-server.md#http-server-a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall)).

**Declined:**
- **No store at all where nothing is written.** It was safe and it was useless: a first program that
  wanted a session had to choose a store and run a shared cache before its first page worked. A file
  in the data folder is coherent across the processes of one machine, which is what the memory
  tier's refusal asks for.
- **A table in a `[db.<name>]` for `db`.** It needs a schema in the operator's database and a grant
  to write it. The data folder's file needs neither, and a deployment with several machines has
  `shared`.
- **A session lock, as PHP's file handler takes.** One slow request would hold every other request
  of that session until it ends ([`http-server/a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole)).

<sub>See also [`http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot), [`http-server/a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole), [`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store), [`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole"></a>

## A session record is loaded once at `start`, written back whole only when it changed, and never locked

`rule:http-server/a-session-is-loaded-once-and-written-whole`

`start` reads the record once; `set`, `remove` and `clear` mutate the copy in the request's own
heap; the record is written back when the program that opened it ends — after any exit hooks,
since a hook is user code that may still write — and immediately for `regenerate` and `destroy`.
**Writing only when the record changed** keeps a read-only request off the write path: a request
that starts a session and reads it makes one round trip, not two.

There is no lock. Two requests writing one session concurrently is last-write-wins over the
**whole record**, and this is stated rather than repaired. On the `db` store each operation is one
statement in its own transaction, so nothing is held between `start` and the write-back, and two
requests of one session never wait for each other. A lock held for the length of a
request is a cross-request channel ([`security/closed-doors`](security.md#security-closed-doors)), and a request that dies holding
one wedges every later request for that session until it expires. The cost belongs to a narrow
case — two concurrent requests that write *different keys* of one session lose one of the two
writes — and an application for which that matters has state that is not session state; locks,
counters and idempotency keys go to the shared tier or the database directly
([`concurrency/cross-request-state-is-explicit`](concurrency.md#concurrency-cross-request-state-is-explicit)).

A cancelled task is the one end that sends nothing, because the send parks.

- **Memory:** one encoded record per request that started a session, released with the request
  heap. Nothing accumulates per session served, so it is O(in-flight).

**Declined:**
- **A per-key write instead of a whole-record one.** It narrows the lost update to the key actually
  contended, but one session becomes many entries, so `clear`, `regenerate` and `destroy` each become
  a multi-key operation, and the shared tier has no multi-key atomic step
  ([`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members)).
- **A request-long lock.** It closes the lost update exactly, but the failure it brings is a wedged
  session, on the request path of every application whether or not it has concurrent writers.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations), [`security/closed-doors`](security.md#security-closed-doors), [`concurrency/cross-request-state-is-explicit`](concurrency.md#concurrency-cross-request-state-is-explicit), [`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster), [`http-server/a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers`](http-server.md#http-server-a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers).</sub>

<a id="http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store"></a>

## `[session] ttl` is written onto the record, an expired record is absent at once, and the SQLite store sweeps by time, never by chance

`rule:http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`

`[session] ttl` is written onto the entry: `SET … PX` on the shared tier, and an `expires_at`
column in the `db` store's SQLite file. An expired record is absent at once, so `load` already
answers it and `start` already issues a fresh id
([`http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations)). On the SQLite file `load` reads only
a row whose `expires_at` is still ahead, so correctness never waits for a sweep. `save` refreshes
the expiry, so `ttl` bounds how long an *untouched* record survives.

The SQLite file deletes its expired rows with one indexed `DELETE … WHERE expires_at <= now`, run
by a write at most once a minute per core. That sweep bounds the file at O(live sessions) rather
than O(sessions ever issued). It is driven by time, never by a chance per request, and it is one
statement on the blocking pool beside the write that ran it.

**Declined:**
- **A probabilistic collection, as PHP's `session.gc_probability`.** Which request pays for it is
  chance, and on a quiet site the expired rows stay for days. A sweep by time costs every core the
  same small delete once a minute.
- **A sweep run by a scheduled job.** It would need a `[[schedule]]` entry nobody wrote, so a
  deployment with no configuration would never sweep.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations), [`http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot), [`http-server/no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store`](http-server.md#http-server-no-session-block-means-the-data-folder-store).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-session-holds-a-secret-only-sealed"></a>

## A user's own secret lives in their session, sealed under a key ring through `setSecret` and `getSecret`

`rule:http-server/a-session-holds-a-secret-only-sealed`

A user's own secret — the access and refresh token a web application holds on their behalf — lives in their
session, through `Core\Session::setSecret(string $key, secret string $value, array<secret bytes> $keys)`
and `Core\Session::getSecret(string $key, array<secret bytes> $keys)`, and only **sealed**. Static like
every member of that class ([`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster)): the session is the request's, not an object
a program holds. The construction is the
cache's ([`concurrency/a-secret-is-cached-only-sealed`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-secret-is-cached-only-sealed)) under the session door's own domain byte, so a
value sealed for a cache never opens as a session value and the reverse.

It is the session and not a cache tier because a cache may evict at any time and a user would be logged out
by a footprint decision. There is no `ttl`: a session value lives as long as its session
([`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store)), and the sealed plaintext carries no expiry of its
own.

**The additional data is the domain byte ‖ the app ‖ the key, and not the session id**, because
`regenerate` issues a new id over the same record and a value bound to the old id would stop opening at
exactly the moment a login hardens. Moving a ciphertext between two sessions takes write access to the
store, which already means owning every session in it.

`get` answers `null` for a sealed value and `set` still refuses a `secret`, so the sealed pair is the only
door here too; a sealed value that does not open under the ring is absent rather than an error. The record
crosses the store as the byte carrier it already is
([`http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations)), so no `secret` reaches the store and
[`security/secret-crosses-no-boundary`](security.md#security-secret-crosses-no-boundary) is unchanged.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/a-secret-is-cached-only-sealed`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-secret-is-cached-only-sealed), [`http-server/a-session-store-answers-four-operations`](http-server.md#http-server-a-session-store-answers-four-operations), [`http-server/session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store`](http-server.md#http-server-session-expiry-belongs-to-the-store), [`security/secret-crosses-no-boundary`](security.md#security-secret-crosses-no-boundary).</sub>

<a id="http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files"></a>

## `Core\Request::files()` yields uploaded parts lazily, one at a time, and is the only way to receive one

`rule:http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`

`Core\Request::files(): Iterable<Part>` yields a request's uploaded parts over [`iteration/two-interfaces`](iteration.md#iteration-two-interfaces)'s protocol as they arrive off the connection, one part at a time. It is single-pass, and consuming it is exclusive with `body()` and `bodyStream()` on the same request. There is no buffered sibling and no other member that answers a part: a `post()` never carries a file field, and a body cannot be walked as parts.

The buffered array is absent on purpose. Choosing between a buffered and a streaming accessor needs a per-part size, and that size is not knowable until the part has been consumed — `Content-Length` describes the whole body, and a client's claim about either is only a claim. An API whose safe path is selected from a fact the caller cannot see is a defect independently of what the unsafe path costs, so the choice is not offered.

**Advancing past an unconsumed part drains it.** Skipping an upload the application does not recognise is simply not touching it; the drained bytes are still charged against `upload_total` ([`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps)). Peak memory for an upload of any size is therefore one chunk per in-flight request, plus whatever a call site explicitly asked to hold through [`http-server/a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways).

The runtime owns the multipart parser for the same reason. A large browser upload is always
multipart, so a raw `bodyStream()` alone would leave an application two choices: buffer it, or write
the multipart framing itself, with boundary detection across chunk edges and per-part headers. A
parser differential is a security property, so that framing is not an application's business.

**Memory:** one wire chunk per in-flight request while a part is read, whatever the size of the
upload. A buffered part costs more than its size: a `bytes` value has its payload inline and cannot
point into another buffer, so a part copied out of an accumulated body holds the body and the copy at
once, and a permitted 2G upload would be a 4G peak.

The cost is usability. Every program that accepts a file writes a loop, which is three lines in the
common case, and one of them is `saveTo`. A slow client still holds a connection for as long as
`body_idle_timeout` allows, and it no longer holds the body.

**Declined:**
- **A buffered `files()` beside the stream.** The choice between the two cannot be made from
  anything the application can observe, as the paragraph above says.
- **Refusing to advance until the application skips a part explicitly.** It turns the ordinary
  "ignore what I do not know" loop into ceremony and prevents no mistake anyone makes.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename), [`http-server/a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways), [`http-server/there-is-no-temp-file`](http-server.md#http-server-there-is-no-temp-file), [`security/request-state-throws-in-an-isolate`](security.md#security-request-state-throws-in-an-isolate), [`iteration/two-interfaces`](iteration.md#iteration-two-interfaces), [`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename"></a>

## A part is a file part iff its `Content-Disposition` carries `filename`; every other part is buffered into `post()`

`rule:http-server/a-part-is-a-file-iff-it-carries-a-filename`

A part is a file part exactly when its `Content-Disposition` carries `filename` — RFC 7578's own distinction, and the only one. Every other part is an ordinary form field: the server buffers it and `Core\Request::post()` reads it exactly as it reads a urlencoded form. A `<form>` with a title, a description and a file is read the way it was written, and the application never reconstructs `post()` out of part order. Those buffered fields are charged against `[limits] request_body`, because form-field text is bytes parsed into memory, which is what that cap means. They are also what a `files()` walk leaves behind: the walk streams the file parts and buffers these, so `post()` after a walk answers out of that hold like any other buffering reader, and needs no carve-out of its own ([`http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it`](http-server.md#http-server-buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it)).

A `Part` answers `name()` (the form's field name), `filename()` (the client's claimed name, never a path) and `contentType()`, all three **`tainted`** and all three members rather than properties. `name` is marked with the other two although the form declared it: a peer is under no obligation to send back the names the form declared, and leaving it plain would have made it the one launderer on the class. `contentType()` answers RFC 7578's default `text/plain` where the part declared none.

A part carries **no `size`**. There is no honest value to put there before the part has been consumed, and inventing one from `Content-Length` is the repair [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused) forbids. The part-count cap of [`errors/multipart-part-count`](errors.md#errors-multipart-part-count) applies unchanged; it bounds bookkeeping, which no byte cap reaches.

**Declined:**
- **A third directive for the buffered form fields.** Its right value is one nobody knows, and it would overlap `request_body` almost entirely.

<sub>See also [`http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`](http-server.md#http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files), [`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps), [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused), [`errors/multipart-part-count`](errors.md#errors-multipart-part-count).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways"></a>

## A part is consumed by `readAll`, by walking `content()`, or by `saveTo`, and each way is bounded

`rule:http-server/a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways`

```nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as $part) {
    $csv = $part->readAll();                          // bounded by request_body
    $big = $part->readAll(max: 200 * 1024 * 1024);    // bounded by [limits] memory
    foreach ($part->content() as $chunk) { … }        // Iterable<bytes>, each tainted
    $part->saveTo($dest, max: 50 * 1024 * 1024);      // straight to disk
}
```

- **`readAll({max?}): tainted bytes`** — with no argument, bounded by `[limits] request_body` and refused past it. An explicit `max` is a count of bytes checked against the request tree's own `[limits] memory` instead. `request_body` governs what arrives unasked; `[limits] memory` governs what the application chooses to hold, which is what leaves a deliberate large buffer expressible while keeping the bare call safe by construction.
- **`content(): Iterable<bytes>`** — the part's chunks, each `tainted`, valid only while this part is the iterator's current one. A part the walk has moved past refuses rather than reading the current one.
- **`saveTo(string $path, {max?, overwrite?})`** — the shorthand for [`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream), to which it delegates under the same bag, and the path nearly every upload takes. Its path is a sink: a `tainted` `filename()` reaching it is a compile error, and `Core\IO::within` is the launderer.

A part's bytes are readable exactly once, in order, whichever of the three consumed them. The buffering-and-streaming split of [`http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it`](http-server.md#http-server-buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it) is about the request body and does not repeat itself here: a part is never held, so `readAll` buffering into the application's own variable leaves nothing behind on the request for a second reader to find. An application that needs two passes buffers with `readAll` or writes the part down first, and now says which.

**Declined:**
- **Streaming only, with no way to read a part into memory.** A small avatar to hash, a CSV about to be parsed or a value for a database column wants bytes, and forcing a loop on them buys no safety once the bound sits at the call site.
- **A `max` required at every `readAll`.** The bare call is already bounded by `request_body`, the cap on every other byte parsed into memory, so the argument would buy visibility and no safety, at one argument per call site.

<sub>See also [`http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`](http-server.md#http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files), [`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps), [`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named).</sub>

<a id="http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps"></a>

## `request_body` caps bytes parsed into memory and `upload_total` caps a streamed multipart body, and both are `[limits]` rows

`rule:http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`

| Directive | Default | Ceiling | Bounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `request_body` | `"8M"` | `"64M"` | **Bytes parsed into memory** — `body()`, a JSON or urlencoded body, a multipart form's buffered fields, a bare `readAll()`. |
| `upload_total` | `"256M"` | `"2G"` | **Total bytes of a streamed multipart body**, consumed parts and drained ones alike. |

Both are rows in the `[limits]`/`[limits.hard]` pair that [`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes) established — a `Runtime` default beside a `System` ceiling per [`config/ceilings-are-their-own-directives`](config.md#config-ceilings-are-their-own-directives) — not a third instance of that pattern. `nvs config dump` prints both where the tree writes them, and this table is the only place their meanings are defined.

The split follows from what the two measure. Content parsed into memory deserves the tighter number, because it is resident and O(in-flight); content streamed to disk deserves a ceiling shaped like what uploads are, because a phone photo is 5–12M and an 8M refusal is advice rather than protection. One number governing both would have to be the larger, and would then license a quarter-gigabyte JSON body parsed wholly into memory on the strength of an argument made about files. [`http-server/upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire`](http-server.md#http-server-upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire) is where the second cap bites.

Both ceilings are numbers of their own, so a `[limits]` or `[app.limits]` value past one is refused
at boot whether or not `[limits.hard]` is written (`crates/nvs-config/src/app.rs`'s `body_caps`).

**Where each is read.** The door applies the global `[limits] upload_total` to a declared length,
because it refuses before a mount is selected (`nvs_config::app::upload_total`). A streamed body is
counted against that value until its first reader claims it, and the claim sets the request's own
value in force, `[app.limits]` and `Core\Config::set` included (`RequestBody::allow_total`).
`request_body` is read off the request by every reader that parses into memory
(`Ctx::request_body_limit`). Neither reads "no cap" from a missing or malformed value: both fall back
to the shipped default.

<sub>See also [`http-server/upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire`](http-server.md#http-server-upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire), [`http-server/a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways), [`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes), [`config/ceilings-are-their-own-directives`](config.md#config-ceilings-are-their-own-directives), [`errors/multipart-part-count`](errors.md#errors-multipart-part-count), [`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps).</sub>

<a id="http-server-upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire"></a>

## `upload_total` is enforced by the server on the wire: a declared oversize is refused before dispatch and a chunked one is stopped at the part being read

`rule:http-server/upload-total-is-enforced-on-the-wire`

`upload_total` is enforced by the server, not by each consumer. A request whose `Content-Length` already exceeds it is answered `413` **before dispatch** — before a mount is selected, before an isolate exists and before any application code runs — so the honest oversized client never reaches a program. A chunked body with no declared length is counted as bytes arrive, and when the total is crossed the iterator throws at the part being read and the connection is closed rather than left half-consumed.

Enforcing in the server rather than at every `readAll` and `content()` is what keeps the streaming path bounded now that it is the only path ([`http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`](http-server.md#http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files)): the parts an application drains without reading are still the server's to count, and a bound placed in the parser would miss exactly the bytes it never sees. The number is load-bearing twice, because a body a request holds is memory that [`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number) counts against the room every later request is admitted into.

<sub>See also [`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps), [`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number), [`security/isolate-budget-is-the-trees`](security.md#security-isolate-budget-is-the-trees), [`http-server/the-server-block-is-boot-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-server-block-is-boot-class).</sub>

<a id="http-server-there-is-no-temp-file"></a>

## There is no temp file: a part lands on disk only where the application names a path under `fs.write`, and disk is the resource it must bound

`rule:http-server/there-is-no-temp-file`

There is no `tmp_name` on a request, no temp directory to configure, permission or defend against symlinks, no window between the runtime writing a file and the application claiming it — so no upload/move race and no `is_uploaded_file` to bypass — and no orphan for the runtime to clean up after a crash. A part that lands on disk lands there because the application named a path through `saveTo` or [`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream) and holds `fs.write`; an upload nobody saves was never on disk at all.

Runtime-managed temp files with a hidden path — the obvious middle road — remove `tmp_name`'s worst edge but keep every operational one: a directory to configure, cleanup after a crash, disk exhaustion under no cap. They buy nothing `saveTo` does not, since the application names a destination anyway.

What this trades is stated rather than implied: **the resource this design can exhaust is disk, and the application owns bounding it.** `writeStream`'s `max` is the per-call bound, `upload_total` ([`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps)) is the per-request one, and neither is a quota over a directory — an operator accepting uploads watches the volume they land on. That is a cost bought with the memory cost it replaces: a permitted 2G upload is no longer a 4G peak per in-flight request.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways`](http-server.md#http-server-a-part-is-consumed-in-one-of-three-ways), [`http-server/request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-request-body-and-upload-total-are-two-caps), [`core-classes/io-write-stream`](core-classes.md#core-classes-io-write-stream), [`security/capability-check-at-the-door`](security.md#security-capability-check-at-the-door), [`http-server/the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps`](http-server.md#http-server-the-body-is-read-on-demand-under-two-caps).</sub>

<a id="http-server-no-spelling-for-an-unbounded-wait"></a>

## `Core\Http\Client` has no spelling for "wait forever": every bound is a `Duration`, an omitted one inherits `[http.client]`, and expiry throws `TimeoutError`

`rule:http-server/no-spelling-for-an-unbounded-wait`

`Core\Http\Client` has no spelling for "wait forever". Every bound in `Core\Http\Options` —
`deadline`, `connectTimeout`, `retryBackoff` — is a `Duration`, which has no infinite value
([`types/duration`](types.md#types-duration)); there is no `deadline: null` and no `0` meaning unbounded; and a
call that omits the field inherits `[http.client] deadline` (shipped `30s`) or `connect_timeout`
(shipped `5s`) rather than removing the bound. An unbounded outbound call is therefore not
something a program can express, the same way a shell string is not something `Core\Process` can
express ([`core-classes/process-is-argv-only`](core-classes.md#core-classes-process-is-argv-only)): the guarantee comes from the absence of a
spelling, not from a check.

A finite default times out a call somebody expected to take five minutes. A long poll or a large
upload names its own `deadline`, which is one field, and having to name it is the point: the
number that bounds a slow dependency is written down where an operator can change it.

The bag is a closed set of keys, and the three retry keys — `retryAttempts`, `retryBackoff`,
`retryIdempotencyKey` — are flat. The prefix keeps the grouping legible at a call site
(`{retryAttempts: 3, retryIdempotencyKey: $key}`).

Expiry throws `TimeoutError`, never a falsy return ([`core-api/failure-throws`](core-api.md#core-api-failure-throws)), and the
deadline it reports is the one that covers the whole call
([`http-server/one-deadline-covers-the-whole-call`](http-server.md#http-server-one-deadline-covers-the-whole-call)).

**Declined:**
- **A nested `retry` shape.** A bag flattens to one ABI argument per option, and a bag nested
  inside one has nothing to flatten into; it would need a runtime shape value on the common path,
  which [`core-api/shape-rules`](core-api.md#core-api-shape-rules) R2 exists to avoid.

<sub>See also [`http-server/one-deadline-covers-the-whole-call`](http-server.md#http-server-one-deadline-covers-the-whole-call), [`http-server/retry-is-opt-in-jittered-and-closed`](http-server.md#http-server-retry-is-opt-in-jittered-and-closed), [`types/duration`](types.md#types-duration), [`core-api/failure-throws`](core-api.md#core-api-failure-throws), [`core-classes/process-is-argv-only`](core-classes.md#core-classes-process-is-argv-only).</sub>

<a id="http-server-an-outbound-request-carries-one-body"></a>

## An outbound request carries at most one body, named by which of four flat keys it is written under, and a second key or a body on `get` is a compile-time diagnostic

`rule:http-server/an-outbound-request-carries-one-body`

An outbound request carries at most one body, and which of four flat keys in `Core\Http\Options` it was
written under is what says how it is sent: `json` encodes the value as `application/json`, `form` encodes
a map as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `body` sends the octets as given under an optional
`contentType`, and `multipart` sends a map as `multipart/form-data`. Four keys rather than one with a
mode beside it, because a mode string is refused ([`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings)) and sniffing cannot
tell a form from a JSON object by looking at an `array<string, string>`.

**Two body keys, a body on `get` or `head`, and `contentType` without `body` are compile-time
diagnostics**, each naming the key. Both halves of the question are in front of the checker: the bag is a
compile-time-constant anonymous object ([`core-api/shape-rules`](core-api.md#core-api-shape-rules) R2) and the verb is the member's own
name, which is exactly why the missing idempotency key is a diagnostic too
([`http-server/a-non-idempotent-retry-needs-an-idempotency-key`](http-server.md#http-server-a-non-idempotent-retry-needs-an-idempotency-key)). Where the verb is dynamic, the same
two checks throw before the first attempt.

A body position admits `tainted`, because posting what a user sent is ordinary and the qualifier is a
question about sinks a request body does not have; and it admits `secret`, as a header already does
([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)'s outbound exemption), which is why a `json` value is walked with
that exemption applied rather than handed to `Core\Json::encode`. `Core\Http\Part` is how a body is sent
without being held: `Part::file` streams from disk under `fs.read` with `Content-Length` from the file's
