The bound is stated because the default it replaces is not: an unbounded pool of threads that each reserve a stack is a footprint that grows with a workload's blocking fan-out rather than with its concurrency. What the pool spends, per [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority): at most that many OS thread stacks per worker, resident only in what a job touches, plus one boxed Rust `FnOnce` per job in flight.

**Declined:**
- **`io_uring` for the blocking paths.** It is faster and would remove the handoff rather than bound it,
  but it is a second I/O model on one platform only, in a workspace that keeps its runtime dependency
  surface narrow. Simplicity outweighs it until a measurement says otherwise.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/the-reactor-reports-readiness`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-reactor-reports-readiness), [`concurrency/the-parking-contract`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-parking-contract), [`concurrency/try-the-syscall-then-park`](concurrency.md#concurrency-try-the-syscall-then-park), [`http-server/a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers`](http-server.md#http-server-a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers), [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-request-that-computes-shares-its-core"></a>

## A request that runs a 10 ms slice without waiting gives its core back at its next safepoint poll, behind readiness

`rule:http-server/a-request-that-computes-shares-its-core`

A core runs one task at a time, and a task runs until it waits. [`http-server/a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall`](http-server.md#http-server-a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall) keeps a core from waiting on the kernel, and [`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper) bounds a request by its own deadline. Neither stops a request that computes and never waits from holding its core for the whole of that deadline, and every other request on the core waits with it.

**A request that has run a time slice of 10 ms without waiting gives its core back at its next safepoint poll, behind every task the reactor has woken since.** It runs again at its next turn, with its memory, its CPU time and its deadline unchanged, so a neighbour on the same core waits at most a slice for each request ahead of it. The slice holds on every core of `nvs serve` and on the thread of `nvs run`.

- **The clock is one thread per process, and it reads epochs, not clocks.** It adds one to an epoch counter every 5 ms while any core is in a turn. A core stores the epoch into its own slot when it resumes a task and clears the slot when the turn ends. A slot two epochs behind has run the slice, and the thread raises the safepoint flag `YIELD` on the request tree that core is running, which the watchdog's record already names (`crates/nvs-host/src/slice.rs`). With every slot clear the thread parks, and the core that starts the next turn wakes it, so an idle server wakes no thread.
- **The yield goes behind readiness.** On a core with a reactor, the yield fires a wake and parks, so the reactor is polled before the request resumes and the accept loop and every connection get their turn. Putting the request back at the front of the run queue would keep the scheduler from ever reaching the reactor while one request spins.
- **The yield is taken inside a helper frame**, as every other suspension from compiled code is, so a teardown at that point never unwinds through compiled frames.
- **The poll is the safepoint poll at a back edge or a function entry, so a slice ends between two calls.** A helper call is one turn: its batched poll reads the deadline alone, and it gives the core back when it returns ([`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper)).
- **A request's accounting stays its own across the switch.** A turn's memory is charged to the request tree that ran it ([`security/isolate-budget-is-the-trees`](security.md#security-isolate-budget-is-the-trees)), and the CPU time is the tree's through the watchdog's meter. A `Core\Task::all` deadline is on the core's reactor, so it stops a task that never waits one slice late at most ([`concurrency/limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds`](concurrency.md#concurrency-limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds)).

What it spends, as [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority) requires: one OS thread per process, parked while no core is in a turn, and one slot per registered thread, O(cores). A resume pays one relaxed load and one sequentially consistent store and load, and the end of a turn one store. Nothing is allocated per turn. A request that computes pays one reactor poll per slice, well under 1% of its time. The poll site is the one compiled code already has: `YIELD` is one more bit in the word every back edge loads, so no codegen changes.

A thread with no per-thread clock publishes no request to the watchdog, so nothing asks it to yield, and a request there keeps its core until it waits or its deadline ends it.

**Declined:**
- **A slice driven by the watchdog's sweep.** The sweep reads each core's thread clock every 500 ms, which is fifty slices. That is far too coarse to share a core, and reading every clock at every tick costs more than the epoch store does.
- **A configuration key for the slice.** A key is one more thing an operator must understand, for a figure nobody tunes per deployment. Go preempts at the same 10 ms, and a slice is long next to the cost of a switch. If a measurement shows `hello` losing more than 3%, the constant becomes 20 ms and this rule says so.
- **Preemption by signal.** A signal interrupts compiled code at any instruction, where no stack map and no consistent value exist, and makes every helper reentrant. The safepoint poll is already at every back edge and function entry, so a cooperative yield there costs nothing new and leaves every value consistent.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers`](http-server.md#http-server-a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers), [`http-server/a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall`](http-server.md#http-server-a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall), [`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper), [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline), [`security/isolate-budget-is-the-trees`](security.md#security-isolate-budget-is-the-trees), [`concurrency/limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds`](concurrency.md#concurrency-limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds), [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline"></a>

## A watchdog reads the in-flight deadline each worker already keeps, and reports a core whose oldest deadline is past by a margin

`rule:http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`

Every other bound answers a fault. None answers a worker that faults in no way at all and simply stops — an engine deadlock, or a loop with no poll site in it that [`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper)'s combinator did not reach.

**A watchdog thread reads the in-flight deadline each worker already maintains** and reports a worker whose oldest in-flight request has passed its deadline by a configured margin, `[server] watchdog_margin`. It costs the worker nothing: it reads state the deadline mechanism keeps anyway, so no heartbeat is written on any hot path. A heartbeat counter stored at the safepoint poll was rejected for exactly that reason — a store on the hottest path in the runtime to produce a fact a cold reader can already derive.

There is one such thread for the process, not one per core, started when the first core registers; it holds one entry per registered core, O(cores), and wakes once per interval to read one atomic per entry. A stall is reported once per deadline rather than once per sweep, because a wedged core republishes nothing and its earliest deadline is a stable identity for the episode. The report goes to [`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor)'s floor, and what happens next is [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed).

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed), [`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper), [`http-server/the-floor-cannot-fill-the-disk`](http-server.md#http-server-the-floor-cannot-fill-the-disk), [`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed"></a>

## A reported core stops accepting and `max_in_flight` counts its share as unavailable; a wedged worker is never killed in-process

`rule:http-server/a-wedged-core-is-shed-never-killed`

What a watchdog report does is **report and shed, never kill**: the affected core stops accepting new work, and `max_in_flight` accounts for its share as unavailable so the remaining cores are not asked to carry a ceiling that assumes it ([`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number)). The watchdog reads the in-flight deadline each worker already keeps, so a worker pays nothing for being watched.

Admission subscribes to the watchdog's report and grows no detector of its own
(`crates/nvs-server/src/admit.rs`). Every sweep writes how many cores are watched, how many are wedged
and each core's own flag. A request on a reported core is refused a place, and the count refuses at
`max_in_flight` less the wedged cores' share, so one wedged core of two halves it and every core wedged
leaves nothing. The sweep that finds the core turning again clears both, and its share returns within
one interval. A request pays one thread-local read and three relaxed loads for it, and the process
holds two counts and one flag per core.

Killing is not available and the rule does not pretend otherwise. A thread cannot be safely killed in-process, and the process boundary that would make it possible is the one [`http-server/the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class) declines. The one process-level end this leaves is the service manager's own, and it is not this rule's kill: a
unit with `WatchdogSec=` set stops a process that has stopped pinging, and
[`packaging/the-generated-unit-is-hardened`](packaging.md#packaging-the-generated-unit-is-hardened) gates that ping on this rule's detector — withheld only
where **no** core is turning, which is a process with nothing left to shed onto and nothing still
serving to be ended. Detection without a kill is still worth its cost: a wedged core that is reported degrades a service measurably, while a wedged core that is silent looks like a capacity problem for as long as anyone is willing to add capacity.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline), [`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number), [`http-server/the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class), [`http-server/the-server-block-is-boot-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-server-block-is-boot-class).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-request-outlives-a-client-that-goes-away"></a>

## A request whose client goes away runs to its end under its `wall_time`, or `disconnect_grace` when it has none, unless its method is listed in `cancel_on_disconnect`

`rule:http-server/a-request-outlives-a-client-that-goes-away`

A request whose client goes away runs to its end, under every limit it already has, and its response is thrown away; a method listed in `[limits] cancel_on_disconnect` is cancelled at the drop instead.

The case it answers: a request hangs on something slow and the user closes the tab. On a server that gives each request a worker process, that request holds the whole process until its time limit, and a handful of them empties the pool for every user at once — the cost that pushes such servers towards cancelling.

**Completion is the default for every method.** A user who refreshes, navigates away or submits twice abandons a request, so a disconnect is the everyday case; cancelling there stops a script between two writes that share no transaction, and leaves half-written data its author never planned for. The cost that argues for cancelling does not exist here: a request waiting on readiness is a parked coroutine ([`http-server/a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall`](http-server.md#http-server-a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall)) costing a pooled stack rather than a worker, and its CPU, memory and output limits still bound it. **A detached request keeps its admission place until it ends** ([`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number)) — giving it back at the drop would let a client open, disconnect and repeat until a core runs unbounded work. Every write it makes to the response, buffered or streamed, succeeds at once and its bytes are discarded; nothing throws because the client left, and a streamed write does not park on a gone socket. A send timeout counts as the client having gone. A read of the request body after the drop fails as any failed read does. `Core\Sse` and a WebSocket are upgraded connections, not requests, and are outside this rule.

**The one bound it adds.** A request with a `wall_time` has that one limit, connected or not. A request without one — the default — is cancelled once `[limits] disconnect_grace` (default `30s`, finite, no unbounded spelling, [`http-server/an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect`](http-server.md#http-server-an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect)) has passed since the disconnect. `wall_time` is a `Runtime` key, so the deadline follows it: from the drop on, a request has exactly one of the two bounds and never neither. A graceful drain waits for a detached request as for an attached one, up to `drain_timeout`.

**A listed method is cancelled at the drop**: the connection lives on the reactor, so its drop is delivered like any other readiness, and the server cancels the request tree — [`concurrency/cancellation-runs-no-user-code`](concurrency.md#concurrency-cancellation-runs-no-user-code)'s cancellation, delivered at the next safepoint, running native teardown and no user code, with a task inside a driver statement drained under [`concurrency/nothing-is-still-running-when-a-call-returns`](concurrency.md#concurrency-nothing-is-still-running-when-a-call-returns). A request past its grace is cancelled the same way. Both keys are `System` keys a request cannot change, matched by exact, case-sensitive method name, and may be written in `[app.limits]` for one application. The method is the switch because it says whether stopping is safe: a `GET` or `HEAD` that writes nothing can stop, and a `POST` should not. `cancel_on_disconnect` defaults to `[]`; a name that is not an HTTP token, or a name listed twice, is refused at load naming the key, and any token is allowed, so a custom method can be listed. `disconnect_grace` refuses `false` and `0` as `[server]`'s waits do, and has no `[limits.hard]` ceiling because no request may set it. There is no runtime switch and no method that tells a script its client has gone.

After the response is on the wire, the connection's end means nothing to the request — the tree outlives it for exactly the work [`concurrency/after-response-outlives-the-connection`](concurrency.md#concurrency-after-response-outlives-the-connection) admits, which a detached request reaches as an attached one does.

- **Memory:** a detached request keeps its heap until it ends, reaches its `wall_time` or, with none, `disconnect_grace`: per request, O(in-flight), and under its own `memory` cap. A request whose client stays pays nothing.

**Declined:**

- **Cancellation at the drop as the default.** The everyday disconnect breaks data, and every application would need the same one line to turn it off.
- **Completion for every request with no opt-out.** A deployment serving expensive read-only searches loses nothing by stopping them, and wants the capacity back.
- **A switch per route or per request.** A route table is not a configuration concept, and a per-request switch is a runtime method this rule does not add.
- **A `Core` method like PHP's `ignore_user_abort()`.** Completion would be something each script must remember, which is the wrong default for the everyday case.
- **Giving the admission place back at the drop.** A disconnect loop becomes unbounded work on one core.
- **A grace on every detached request, `wall_time` or not.** One request would have two limits, and a long job would be cut short because its client left.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/cancellation-runs-no-user-code`](concurrency.md#concurrency-cancellation-runs-no-user-code), [`concurrency/after-response-outlives-the-connection`](concurrency.md#concurrency-after-response-outlives-the-connection), [`concurrency/nothing-is-still-running-when-a-call-returns`](concurrency.md#concurrency-nothing-is-still-running-when-a-call-returns), [`http-server/a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall`](http-server.md#http-server-a-core-is-never-blocked-on-a-syscall), [`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number), [`http-server/an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect`](http-server.md#http-server-an-unsafe-or-unbounded-default-is-a-defect).</sub>

<a id="http-server-every-deadline-is-monotonic"></a>

## Every timeout, deadline and backoff in the engine is computed on a monotonic clock

`rule:http-server/every-deadline-is-monotonic`

Every timeout, deadline and backoff in the engine is computed on a monotonic clock, never on wall time. A wall-clock deadline is disabled by a clock step, and a step is not an exotic event — it is what happens the first time an instance synchronises time after a long boot.

This is a substitution rather than an addition, and it is stated only because the failure it prevents is silent: a deadline on the wrong clock does not fire late, it does not fire at all. The watchdog of [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline) reads the same monotonic instants, so a stepped clock cannot make a healthy core look wedged or a wedged one look healthy.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline), [`http-server/time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-time-is-bounded-inside-a-helper), [`concurrency/limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds`](concurrency.md#concurrency-limit-and-deadline-are-the-only-bounds).</sub>

<a id="http-server-the-floor-cannot-fill-the-disk"></a>

## The floor cannot fill the disk it writes to: a file target rotates under a retention bound, repeats coalesce into one record with a count, and a cache write failure compiles in memory

`rule:http-server/the-floor-cannot-fill-the-disk`

[`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor)'s floor writes unconditionally, which is correct, and a request that faults in a loop therefore writes in a loop. Two bounds, both on the **sink** rather than on the callers, so that no caller has to be trusted to be rare:

- **Rotation and a retention bound** on any file target, for the diagnostic log and the access log alike. `[log] max_size` (default `"10M"`, above zero) is the size at which the file becomes `<file>.1` and older files shift up; `[log] keep` (default `5`, zero allowed) is how many shifted files stay, and `keep = 0` deletes the full file. Everything a target can occupy is `(keep + 1) × max_size`, and the bound is enforced before the write so a record never straddles two files. Every writer in the process that names one path shares one file and one in-memory count, so the bound is per file. A rotation that fails keeps the record in the live file, warns once, and is tried again after another `max_size`: losing records would hide the failure the floor is reporting.
- **A rate limit with a coalescing counter** — repeated identical records within a window become one record carrying a count. The record shape is [`errors/diagnostic-record`](errors.md#errors-diagnostic-record)'s and gains a `count` field rather than a second shape; it is the one key written by a sink rather than by a producer. The next occurrence after the window carries how many it stands for, and a record that differs is never held back.

A full disk also stops compilation, which would convert a log problem into a total outage. **A write failure in the on-disk artifact cache falls back to compiling in memory** and reports once; the cache is an optimisation and is treated as one.

The request path pays one lock and one comparison per record written to a file, and the size is counted in memory with no `stat` per record.

- **Memory:** one shared entry per open log path, per process.

<sub>See also [`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor), [`errors/diagnostic-record`](errors.md#errors-diagnostic-record), [`errors/renderings`](errors.md#errors-renderings), [`http-server/the-accept-loop-backs-off`](http-server.md#http-server-the-accept-loop-backs-off), [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline), [`packaging/an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file`](packaging.md#packaging-an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file).</sub>

<a id="http-server-a-jit-page-is-never-writable-and-executable-at-once"></a>

## A page holding generated code is writable while written and executable only after being made read-only

`rule:http-server/a-jit-page-is-never-writable-and-executable-at-once`

Pages holding generated code are mapped writable while being written and executable only after being made read-only. The transition is one call per compiled unit, on the compile pool, at compile time; a loaded artifact is copied into a private writable region, relocated there, and only then made executable, so a verified-but-writable mapping is never the one that runs.

This is a security property before it is a stability one — a page that is both writable and executable is a write primitive for any bug that reaches it — and it sits with the server rules because the JIT is this runtime's distinguishing component and nothing else owns the question.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers`](http-server.md#http-server-a-requests-blast-radius-is-bounded-at-four-tiers), [`http-server/the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class), [`programs/compile-target`](programs.md#programs-compile-target).</sub>

<a id="http-server-the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class"></a>

## A memory-safety fault in `unsafe` code or a miscompile is the one residue: the process dies, the supervisor restarts it, and the answer is frequency, not a boundary

`rule:http-server/the-residue-is-one-named-fault-class`

What survives every other bound is **a memory-safety fault in `unsafe` code, or a miscompilation from the code generator**. Neither is containable in-process: `catch_unwind` does not catch a `SIGSEGV`, and wrong machine code has already done whatever it does before any check runs.

**A Rust panic is never part of the residue.** Every Rust entry compiled code calls with a context
runs inside `catch_unwind`: each helper through `run_helper`, including its memory pre-check and
collection, and the safepoint and stack-check slow paths through `abi::contain_panic`, including the
collection and the limit handler's runtime half. A panic there ends its one request with a `FATAL`,
and the next request on the core is answered. Code with no request beneath it is contained at the
task root ([`http-server/containment-does-not-end-at-the-helper`](http-server.md#http-server-containment-does-not-end-at-the-helper)). The primitives that carry no
context, such as `nvs_array_set`, call no user code and have no wrap. An unwind that reaches a JIT
frame aborts the process, so a panic in one of them is a bug to fix, not a fault class to contain.

For these, tier D applies: the process dies, the supervisor restarts it, the requests in flight are lost, and recovery takes about a cold start — a figure that is, for this runtime, unusually small. A worker-process boundary under a supervisor was the alternative examined hardest and it does not pay: a refcount fault means one request reads another's memory, and N processes lower that probability without eliminating it; a deterministic miscompile on one route kills every process in turn; and the compiled-unit cache, the connection-pool sizing and the topic broadcast would all be duplicated or turned cross-process for a benefit that is narrow and partly theoretical. It is reopened when persistent connections ship, because a server holding many live connections that dies is a different event from a request server that dies.

The engineering response to this class is **not** a boundary; it is to reduce the rate at which the class occurs — the conformance cases run against generated code at every optimisation level, fuzzing the code generator the way the lexer and parser are fuzzed, and running the reference-counting paths under `tools/leak-check.sh`. A fault class that cannot be contained is one whose frequency is the only variable left.

Before any worker count above one is recommended, two numbers have to be measured: the per-unit size of
compiled code, which sets the duplicated cache's footprint, and the per-unit compilation time, which
sets the warm-up cost. A cold start bounds them jointly and separates neither.

**Declined:**
- **Process-per-request.** It is the only arrangement that contains a disclosure fault, and it discards
  the thread-per-core runtime the whole performance design rests on. It is the endpoint of the
  worker-process argument above, not a close call.
